evaluation.positioning_hook: A grieving undead cop in a segregated monster city uncovers a police conspiracy that turns his own precinct into a factory for controlled zombies, forcing him to choose between the law and the living.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has an immediate sell: a cop thriller inside a monster society, with clear action, horror, and conspiracy hooks. The audience is real and genre-friendly, though the dense worldbuilding and hard-R violence narrow it from four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands fast in the opening pages: a vampire assault, an armored undead cop, and a precinct that literally separates the dead battery from the live battery. The script keeps the premise legible even as it expands into the Re-Life conspiracy.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Helm is a strong anchor: stoic, wounded, religious, and morally rigid, with a clear emotional fracture around his dead wife. Foster, Reynolds, and Beacon each add distinct pressure, but Helm remains the only truly durable center of gravity.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s central invention is bold: a noir police procedural where zombies, vampires, and werewolves are integrated into civic labor and law enforcement. The dead-battery/live-battery bureaucracy gives the material a fresh satirical edge without losing genre momentum.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story moves through a sequence of patrol calls, each escalating the mystery of the missing chips and the changing monster behavior. The middle is episodic by design, but the conspiracy thread and Beacon reveal give the back half a strong pull.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script’s most resonant idea is also its cleanest: a cop who executes monsters under a legal code while the system quietly manufactures them. That contradiction feels both surprising and inevitable once the Re-Life program is revealed.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Dead Battery feels operational, not decorative: precinct hierarchy, Re-Life paperwork, the Crypt, the Holding Tower, the live/dead battery split, and the monster labor economy all generate story. The world has rules and social friction that keep producing new scenes.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is a workable blend of hard-boiled police banter, grotesque body horror, and deadpan civic absurdity. It is specific enough to stand out, though the script occasionally leans more on premise than on a fully singular tonal signature.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the monster-action surface, the script is about grief, institutional violence, and the moral cost of order. The Re-Life conspiracy and Beacon’s ideology suggest a larger political engine, even if the feature format keeps most of that in thriller mode.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Helm/Foster is a strong lead-partner engine, and Reynolds, Beacon, Paddy, and Cara each create meaningful pressure points. It is not a sprawling ensemble, but the relationships are active enough to keep the precinct world generating scenes.

lead_characters.name: Luke Helm
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, undead police officer, white, physically imposing, widower, religious.
lead_characters.hook: A hard-edged public servant in the dead battery, Helm is a disciplined, grief-struck cop who treats monsters like any other criminal and hides his pain behind procedure, faith, and violence. His cross tattoos and church visits signal a man trying to keep a moral center in a world that has already buried him once.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Karl Urban in Dredd or Josh Brolin in Sicario — a stoic, physically authoritative lead who can carry action, moral ambiguity, and buried grief without ever over-explaining himself.

lead_characters.name: Thomas Foster
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s-30s, living human police officer, white, rookie transfer from the live battery.
lead_characters.hook: Foster is the audience surrogate and moral pressure valve: earnest, observant, and increasingly horrified by what the dead battery considers normal. He starts as Helm’s rookie partner and ends up the story’s most volatile wildcard, driven by his sister’s captivity and his own compromised choices.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Aaron Paul in Breaking Bad or Jesse Plemons in Fargo a chance to play innocence curdling under pressure — a reactive part that turns into a betrayal engine.

lead_characters.name: Commissioner Beacon
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s-60s, undead authority figure, white, senior police administrator.
lead_characters.hook: Beacon is the smiling civic father of the precinct, a bureaucrat with predator instincts who uses charm, policy, and institutional trust as camouflage. Once revealed, he becomes the story’s ideological villain: a man who believes control is the only honest form of order.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-reveal authority role that lets an actor play warmth, menace, and institutional rot in the same performance — the showcase lane of Giancarlo Esposito in Breaking Bad or Michael Emerson in Person of Interest.

lead_characters.name: Alicia Reynolds
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s-40s, living human chief coroner, white, recent widow.
lead_characters.hook: Reynolds enters as a competent outsider with a professional spine and quickly becomes Helm’s emotional counterweight and investigative ally. She is practical, grieving, and quietly brave, with the kind of calm intelligence that makes her dangerous to a corrupt system.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong prestige-supporting territory in the vein of Vera Farmiga in Bates Motel or Carrie Coon in The Leftovers — a role that gives an actor intelligence, restraint, and emotional fracture without needing constant fireworks.

lead_characters.name: Paddy McCallum
lead_characters.demographics: Male, middle-aged, city medical examiner, white, human.
lead_characters.hook: Paddy is the precinct’s deadpan forensic conscience, a working-class technician who understands the system’s rot before anyone else does. His death is the story’s first real warning that the conspiracy is not theoretical.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact but memorable character-actor role in the tradition of John C. Reilly in Magnolia or David Harbour in early prestige ensemble work — a grounded, humane presence whose death changes the board.

lead_characters.name: Cara
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s, incarcerated human woman, addict, Foster’s sister.
lead_characters.hook: Cara is the emotional hostage that gives Foster’s betrayal its force: sharp-tongued, wounded, and trapped in a system that has already decided her fate. Her prison scene gives the script its clearest family pressure and its most painful moral leverage.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of brief but devastating role that can become a calling card if played with rawness — the showcase lane of a scene-stealing turn like Jena Malone in Donnie Darko or Kaitlyn Dever in short-form prestige drama.

lead_characters.name: Ronald Ho
lead_characters.demographics: Male, adult, Hawaiian, public servant, rotund build.
lead_characters.hook: Ho is a vivid precinct regular whose gruesome death helps establish the stakes and the rules of the world. He is more texture than arc, but he deepens the sense of a functioning workplace under siege.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of character-actor role that lets someone land a memorable, quotable precinct presence in the mold of a David Zayas or Luis Guzmán supporting turn.

lead_characters.name: Thelma Louise
lead_characters.demographics: Female, adult, undead domestic abuse victim, wife.
lead_characters.hook: Thelma Louise is a one-scene domestic tragedy that turns the script’s monster premise into a relationship problem with teeth. Her name, her bruises, and her grief make the world feel lived-in and cruelly ordinary.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sharp, emotionally legible cameo with a horror twist — the kind of role that lets an actor make a lasting impression in a single scene, like a memorable guest turn in an anthology or prestige genre film.

lead_characters.name: Maria Cruz
lead_characters.hook: Maria Cruz is a civilian witness whose broken-English plea and damaged home ground the monster chaos in neighborhood reality. She gives the patrol work a social texture beyond the precinct.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a useful, grounded supporting role for a strong character actor — the kind of part that benefits from specificity and can anchor a scene without needing a large footprint.

casting_characteristics: Lead requires a physically imposing actor who can play stoicism and grief
Multiple monster roles require prosthetics or makeup performance
Beacon needs an actor who can pivot from genial authority to predatory menace
Reynolds and Foster need strong chemistry for the emotional and investigative spine

notable_requirements: Police precinct with administrative and holding areas

technical.vfx_details: Creature transformations, disintegration effects, energy-hole vortex, sensor POV overlays, and a few monster reveal shots; most effects are practical-forward but require digital cleanup and enhancement.
technical.sfx_needs: Blood squibs, body-part gags, prosthetic monster makeup, dismemberment effects, and practical burn/disintegration setups.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: genre-forward theatrical or streamer-premiere with horror-action positioning.

budget.note: Creature makeup, disintegration effects, a subterranean lab set, and multiple night exteriors are the main cost drivers; the script is not effects-heavy enough to become a VFX picture, but it is beyond a cheap contained indie.

casting.note: The project lives or dies on Helm: the role needs physical authority, dry humor, and wounded interiority. Beacon and Reynolds also need actors who can sell the tonal pivot from procedural banter to conspiracy thriller.

development.note: The world is clear, but the script’s many patrol-call set pieces and the Re-Life conspiracy need disciplined feature shaping so the investigation feels cumulative rather than episodic.

comp_set.title: Dredd
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the armored lawman energy, brutal urban enforcement, and comic-book severity of a cop who treats a hostile city as a battlefield.

comp_set.title: Bright
comp_set.why_it_comps: The same basic commercial idea of a modern police world populated by fantasy species, with procedural beats layered over species politics and social segregation.

comp_set.title: The Hidden
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the buddy-cop-plus-creature-investigation structure and the escalating sense that the city’s criminal problem is actually a species problem.

comp_set.title: Blade
comp_set.why_it_comps: The hybrid of urban monster action, noir attitude, and a protagonist who moves through a hidden supernatural underworld with lethal competence.

audience_target.primary_audience: Genre fans who want a hard-edged monster cop movie with a conspiracy engine and a morally bruised lead.
audience_target.demographics: Adults 18-49, male-skewing but with crossover appeal for horror-thriller audiences; strongest with viewers who like elevated genre, creature features, and antihero procedurals.

budget_tier.note: Creature effects, multiple monster types, night work, and a handful of specialty sets push this above micro/indie, but the story remains contained enough to avoid studio-scale spend.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals execs buying adult monster IP
indie genre financiers looking for a contained franchise seed
mid-budget action producers with horror taste
international sales buyers who like high-concept creature hooks
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where worldbuilding, violence, and a strong central cop role can sell the package before the cast is fully locked. The precinct setting and monster bureaucracy give it a hook that is easy to market and easy to trailer.

ip_potential.detail: The dead-battery/live-battery world can support sequels and spin-off cases, especially if Helm remains the anchor and the precinct’s monster ecology is expanded into new jurisdictions or divisions.

strengths.what_it_means: This creates a marketable hook that is instantly legible in a pitch and visually trailer-friendly on first contact. Buyers looking for a fresh genre lane get a built-in world with rules, hierarchy, and conflict.
strengths.evidence: The dead battery/live battery split, monster labor roles, and precinct bureaucracy are established early and repeatedly.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Helm is a strong franchise-grade lead
strengths.what_it_means: A stoic, grief-haunted enforcer gives the project a face that can carry action, horror, and moral conflict without needing a huge ensemble. That is the kind of role that attracts actor attachment and gives the movie a durable center.
strengths.evidence: His church ritual, wife flashbacks, and refusal to drink all define a man trying to survive his own history.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The conspiracy reveal is commercially clean
strengths.what_it_means: The Re-Life twist turns the movie from episodic monster policing into a conspiracy thriller with a clear villain and a clear institutional betrayal. That gives the back half a stronger trailer promise and a more satisfying buyer pitch.
strengths.evidence: Beacon’s underground lab, the missing chips, and the revelation that he is manufacturing controlled monsters.

strengths.what_it_means: Helm, Foster, Reynolds, and Beacon create a usable triangle of trust, suspicion, and betrayal that keeps the story from becoming a one-note creature feature. That relationship web is what gives the script repeatable scene energy.
strengths.evidence: Foster’s betrayal, Reynolds’ alliance, and Beacon’s fatherly authority all shift the emotional balance.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone has a sellable edge
strengths.what_it_means: The script mixes deadpan police banter with grotesque monster violence in a way that feels marketable to adult genre buyers. That tonal blend is a real differentiator in a crowded horror-thriller field.
strengths.evidence: The domestic-dispute execution, the zombie prostitute, and the adult-bookstore raid all play as grimly comic and nasty.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, high-concept monster-cop feature with a real lead role and a clean conspiracy engine, which makes it attractive to genre buyers looking for something trailerable and actor-friendly. The world is specific enough to feel franchise-capable, but the movie still reads as a finite, producible package rather than a sprawling effects swing.

items.area: The middle plays like patrol episodes.
items.detail: A long stretch of calls — domestic dispute, alley search, gang bust, vice raid — gives the world texture, but it also risks feeling modular before the Re-Life conspiracy fully takes over. For a feature buyer, that means the script needs confidence that the investigation is accumulating rather than simply touring the city.

items.area: Helm is the only fully durable lead.
items.detail: Foster, Reynolds, and Beacon are vivid, but the movie is structurally Helm’s story; the package depends on one actor carrying the emotional and action load. That is a real strength if cast well, and a real dependency if the role is not locked early.

items.area: The violence is hard-R and often graphic.
items.detail: Disintegrations, eviscerations, severed hands, necrophilia imagery, and body-horror creature work push the material firmly into mature territory. That is fine for streaming or premium buyers, but it narrows the theatrical lane and will shape how the movie is positioned.

The dead battery, live battery, Re-Life, tracking chips, and monster origin history all need the audience to absorb a lot of civic mythology quickly. The script is clear enough on the page, but a buyer will notice that the concept depends on disciplined exposition management.

issues.headline: The main friction is structural: the script spends a lot of time proving out the precinct world before the conspiracy fully locks in, so the feature has to earn its momentum in the middle. The other major conversation is packaging reality — this is a hard-R monster movie with a single load-bearing lead, which is a strong lane, but a lane with real casting and buyer constraints.
